slides.title: A Pitch Email *Under 200 Words* That Gets Replies

slides.label: of journalists prefer pitches *under 200 words*
slides.body: A pitch is an invitation, not the release itself. The details live behind a link.

slides.title: The *4-Line* Structure
items: Line 1 — why it matters to their beat or readers
Line 2 — the news in one sentence (with a number)
Line 3 — what you can offer: data, a spokesperson, photos
Line 4 — link to the full release + your contact
"Data: 3 in 5 Melbourne cafés lifted prices this quarter"

slides.label: follow-up, *3–7 days* later
slides.body: 50% of journalists say one follow-up is ideal. 51% want it 3–7 days after the pitch. More than that is noise.

slides.title: A Template *You Can Use Today*
slides.ex:
Hi (name), I read your piece on (topic) last week.
(Company) has just (the news in one sentence + a number).
We can share (full data / an interview / photos) this week.
Release & images: (link). Thanks — (name, number)

slides.title: Short Pitch, *Better Odds*
items: Send it to whoever handles media relations

captions_meta.li_hook:
The pitches journalists reply to are usually shorter than you think.
According to Muck Rack, 69% of journalists prefer pitches under 200 words.
li_body: The most common mistake we see: pasting the whole release into the pitch. A pitch is an invitation to read, not the release itself.
The same Muck Rack State of Journalism 2025 data settles the follow-up question too: 50% of journalists say one follow-up is ideal, and 51% want it 3–7 days later.
A four-line structure your team can use straight away:
li_points: Relevance: why this topic fits their beat or readers.
The news in one sentence, with a number.
The offer: data, a spokesperson or photos that are ready now.
A link to the full release and a contact who responds.
captions_meta.li_close: The full template is on slide 6. How long are your team's pitches right now?
